title: Poppy's Wobbly Tail Surprise
markdown:
Poppy the squirrel had a tail like a grand banner and a fluttery worry parked in her chest as if it paid rent. Life was best when it was neat: acorns stacked, rustles announced in advance. A sudden sound sent her paws twitching. The worry had strong opinions.

One sun-drenched morning a peculiar carriage rumbled into the Willow Creek clearing, painted like a sunset that had argued with a jam jar: lemon yellow, raspberry pink stripes. Out stepped Madame Petunia, an artist whose hat seemed to be hosting a convention for every colourful feather in the sky. She had come to capture the sparkle of the creek for the Autumn Festival.

A flutter ran through the forest folk. A portrait! Her brush danced across a board that smelled of linseed and festival. A magnificent bear appeared with a nose like a ripe plum, so plump the cubs asked if they might borrow it. A fox whose whiskers seemed to slice moonlight sat so still a moth landed on the paint and was painted in. Each creature beamed as if beaming were the sitting fee. Poppy counted the finished jewels from her branch and lost count, which was unlike her.

Poppy watched from a high branch, heart doing a pitter-patter that would not sit still. A portrait of her? What if she squinted? What if the banner-tail did a silly flip-flop in front of the whole festival?

Madame Petunia’s eyes twinkled like dewdrops. “And now, our shy friend. Let us capture the gentle spirit.”

Poppy’s paws felt stuck in sap. She took a shaky breath; her nose twitched. She tried to hold perfectly still. The tail, sensing the unease, gave a tiny ungraceful wobble. The artist’s sharp eyes noticed.

Swift strokes. The other portraits were jewels. When she held up Poppy’s drawing, a hush fell thicker than morning mist. Then giggles.

The sketch showed one enormous eye staring in surprise and the other squeezed shut in fright. The magnificent tail was a tiny crooked loop, like a dropped button. Not graceful. Poppy, when the world felt a bit too loud.

Her cheeks went berry-red. Whiskers trembled. She wanted to melt into the bark.

“Don’t fret,” chirped Jun the mole, popping from his tunnel. “My tunnels never go quite straight. That’s how I dig.”

Uncle Theo, the old badger, chuckled, pebbles rolling. “Madame Petunia has captured something lively. Perhaps the tail is just shy of the spotlight.” He winked, which in badger is a whole paragraph.

Poppy looked again. The big eye stared. The lopsided tail seemed to tiptoe away. A tiny giggle bubbled, then grew, joined by the others, a warm shared burst.

She took another breath, this one more breeze than squeak. “It does look like me when I’m trying not to worry about a strange cloud. Or a wobbly tail.”

Madame Petunia sparkled. “Truth, spoken with a smile, is a delightful sitting. Tomorrow we sketch the tail looking magnificent. For balance.”

Poppy, who had thought truth had to be serious and stacked like acorns, discovered it could also be a crooked loop on paper that made the whole clearing kinder. The flutter still visited — that was the squirrel in her. When a worry tried to droop the banner, she pictured the surprised eye and the dropped-button tail, and a smile tickled the whiskers.

She logged sap-paws / one-eye sketch / Jun’s crooked tunnels in an acorn-cap notebook, left the drawing pinned where the festival committee could giggle on purpose, and let Uncle Theo inspect the carriage stripes as if badgers judged paint. Jun offered to dig her a straighter sitting-platform and then, grinning, dug a wiggly one instead. Madame Petunia packed the plum-nose bear and promised tomorrow’s magnificent tail, for balance. Poppy’s banner, still a banner, wobbled once, on purpose, and the clearing did not end.
